title: Where the limit becomes visible
dek: A finite Saturday edition on the cost limit of autonomous AI research, Europe’s next shared AI machine, imminent AI-label rules, local coding agents for protected data, evolvable proteins, contagious cancer in fish, heat that travels in rays, an insect’s internal compass, faster hologram rendering, audio watermarks that survive compression, and spatial sound for accessible dialogue scenes.

items.title: METR puts autonomous AI optimization’s useful budget below $3,000
items.summary: METR compared what humans and AI agents achieve for the same money on a real model-training optimization problem. Current agents helped at small budgets, but their advantage ended somewhere between zero and $3,000.
items.body:
METR calls the crossover an “expenditure horizon”. Instead of asking whether an agent beats one benchmark score, it plots improvement against the full cost of model calls, experiments, and human work.

For the NanoGPT speedrun, interviews and code analysis suggested that a one-per-cent training-time improvement costs roughly 16 hours or $2,500 of human labour. Six agent runs spent more than $10,000 in total, yet their estimated expenditure horizons remained between zero and $3,000.

Revalidation erased apparent gains from GPT-5 and Opus 4.1, while GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 made significant but modest improvements. The result covers one small training task, excludes human-AI teams, and may be affected by an inefficient harness or undisclosed training exposure.
items.why_selected: It replaces a vague claim that AI accelerates AI research with a cost curve, then shows exactly where the current evidence stops supporting that claim.

citations.title: Expenditure Horizon: Measuring Optimization Ability, with an Application to NanoGPT

items.title: MeluXina-AI contract adds 1,008 GPUs to Europe’s shared compute
items.summary: EuroHPC has signed an €80 million contract for an AI supercomputer in Luxembourg with 1,008 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. Startups, smaller companies, and researchers are intended users, so the practical test is whether shared European compute becomes easier to access.
items.body:
E4 Computer Engineering will acquire, install, and maintain MeluXina-AI. EuroHPC will fund half of the €80 million budget, with installation expected to start in autumn 2026.

The system will spread 252 liquid-cooled GB200 NVL4 nodes across two Luxembourg sites. EuroHPC estimates a peak AI performance above 20 exaflops and says the machine will support training, testing, and pre-production deployment through isolated multi-tenant environments.

The headline performance is an estimate, not a measured application result. EuroHPC has not given an operational date, so prospective users still do not know when the promised capacity will become available.
items.why_selected: It turns European “sovereign AI” from a strategy document into a contracted machine with a price, hardware count, access model, and installation window.

citations.title: EuroHPC JU signs contract for MeluXina-AI

items.title: EU AI labels become mandatory on 2 August
items.summary: The European Commission has clarified the AI Act transparency rules that start on 2 August 2026. Products must disclose direct AI interaction, generators must embed machine-readable marks, and professional publishers face separate visible-label duties.
items.body:
Providers of chatbots, agents, and avatars must tell people from the first interaction that they are dealing with AI, unless that is already obvious. Providers of generative systems must make synthetic audio, images, video, and text detectable through effective machine-readable marks.

Deployers have a different job. They must visibly or audibly disclose deepfakes and label AI-generated public-interest text unless it received substantive human review and editorial control; spell-checking alone does not qualify.

Source code, machine-to-machine output, closed-loop development material, and standard editing can fall outside the marking duty. Enforcement is split among national authorities and EU bodies, so teams that do not follow the voluntary code may have to prove equivalent compliance case by case.
items.why_selected: It gives European product and media teams an immediate checklist and separates three duties that are easy to confuse: interface disclosure, embedded provenance, and visible publication labels.

citations.title: Guidelines on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
Transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act

items.title: Local open-weight coding agents complete 87.9% of data-prep tasks
items.summary: Researchers tested whether coding agents can clean sensitive study data without sending it to a cloud model. Open-weight models with 31 to 35 billion parameters completed up to 87.9% of a new benchmark on locally controlled hardware.
items.body:
The benchmark turns cleaning scripts for six sweeps of a British cohort study into 20 tasks covering 102 variables. Tasks include harmonizing categories and merging records across different survey waves.

The framework runs the agent against a known correct dataset, then checks both its R code and the data it produces. This matters for health and population research, where governance rules can forbid sending personal data to an external model provider.

The result is author-reported from a new preprint and one carefully curated workflow. It shows that local agents can be useful in this setting, not that they can safely clean arbitrary research data without expert review.
items.why_selected: It gives open-weight models a concrete advantage beyond ideology: they can bring agentic coding into data environments that cloud systems are not allowed to enter.

items.title: AI-redesigned enzymes reach 79-fold higher target specificity after evolution
items.summary: Researchers used an AI model to stabilize enzymes before evolving them in the laboratory. The stronger starting points reached useful protein variants that the natural enzymes could not, including one with more than 79 times greater target specificity.
items.body:
ProteinMPNN redesigned the sequences of three botulinum neurotoxin proteases while preserving their catalytic function and improving stability. The researchers then evolved the redesigned and natural versions side by side using phages that repeatedly mutate and select proteins.

Across four campaigns, the redesigned enzymes adapted faster and reached mutations that failed in the natural protein backgrounds. One redesigned protease evolved to cut ataxin-2 while minimizing its original target, producing more than 79-fold greater selected specificity than the best variant evolved from the natural enzyme.

The work shows a way to give laboratory evolution more room to explore, not a finished therapy. The experiments covered three related enzymes, and every useful design still required physical selection and validation.
items.why_selected: The AI did not guess the final answer. It changed the starting landscape so ordinary evolution could reach answers that were previously inaccessible.

citations.title: AI-redesigned starting points and outcomes enhance protein evolution

items.title: Catfish melanoma is the first transmissible cancer documented in fish
items.summary: Melanomas in Lake Memphremagog catfish are not separate cancers caused by the same pollution or pathogen. Genome sequencing shows that the cancer cells themselves form one infectious lineage moving between fish.
items.body:
Raised black tumours affected 23 to 37% of sampled brown bullheads between 2014 and 2017. Researchers compared each tumour with normal tissue from its host and with tumours from other fish.

The tumour genomes were more closely related to one another than to the fish carrying them. Hundreds of thousands of shared variants appeared in the tumours but not their hosts, which is the signature expected when living cancer cells pass between animals.

This is the first documented transmissible cancer in fish and only the fourth animal group known to harbour one. Its origin, method of transmission, geographic range, and long-term effect on the population remain unknown.
items.why_selected: One clean genetic comparison overturns the intuitive model of cancer as a disease that always begins inside each individual.

citations.title: Brown bullhead catfish melanoma represents a novel transmissible cancer

items.title: Boron arsenide sends heat along rays at room temperature
items.summary: Heat normally spreads out, but researchers mapped narrow, directional temperature patterns in boron arsenide at room temperature. The effect suggests that crystal structure could eventually route heat rather than merely conduct it away.
items.body:
In a solid, heat is carried partly by phonons, waves of atomic vibration. “Phonon focusing” happens when a crystal’s structure sends many of those waves along preferred directions, forming ray-like paths.

Previous observations required cryogenic temperatures. Tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy now mapped the effect at nanoscale resolution in room-temperature boron arsenide, and the patterns matched first-principles transport simulations.

Changing the crystal orientation changed the symmetry and direction of the heat paths across multiple samples. This is still a material-specific laboratory result, not a cooling component, but it makes directional heat control plausible under ordinary conditions.
items.why_selected: It makes an invisible transport process visually intelligible and turns crystal orientation into a possible engineering control for heat.

items.title: Fruit flies remember the direction back to a lost odour plume
items.summary: Fruit flies do more than react when a smell disappears. In a controlled virtual odour world, they stored a direction back to the plume’s edge and updated that internal compass as they moved.
items.body:
Head-fixed flies walked on an air-supported ball while a moving nozzle controlled wind direction and odour concentration. This let the researchers create precise chemical landscapes that would be impossible to see or stabilize in open air.

The flies tracked an attractive plume by repeatedly leaving it and making directed returns to its boundary. Behavioural models, calcium imaging, and neural perturbations pointed to FC2 neurons in the fan-shaped body as the signal for the direction back.

The memory appeared to encode direction, not distance. The experiment shows a reusable navigation strategy in tethered flies, but whether freely moving animals use the same calculation in a turbulent natural plume remains unresolved.
items.why_selected: It reveals a small internal map inside a tiny brain through an experiment that makes an invisible smell landscape measurable.

citations.title: A vector-based strategy for olfactory navigation in Drosophila

items.title: Multiplane images make hologram rendering up to 250,000 times faster
items.summary: A new wave-optics pipeline converts layered 3D images into holograms without calculating every scene primitive separately. The authors report speedups as high as 250,000 times while retaining comparable image quality.
items.body:
A multiplane image stores a scene as a stack of partly transparent pictures at different depths. The new method propagates light from those planes to synthesize the interference pattern needed by a holographic display.

That layered representation avoids the cost of treating millions of points or polygons as separate wave sources. In the authors’ tests, it greatly outpaced primitive-based computer-generated holography and produced better images than conventional layer-based methods.

The team tested simulated scenes and experimentally captured focal stacks and light fields. The maximum speedup depends on the scene and comparison method, and the paper does not show a production display running the pipeline in everyday use.
items.why_selected: It connects a simple visual representation, stacked transparent images, to a very large computational consequence for emerging 3D displays.

citations.title: Fast Wave-optics Rendering of Multiplane Images for 3D Holographic Displays

items.title: Latent audio watermarks survive neural compression with a quality trade-off
items.summary: Researchers embedded a 32-bit watermark inside an audio model’s hidden representation instead of adding it only to the waveform. Codec-aware training raised recovery accuracy from 78.8% to as high as 97.1%, but audibly relevant quality scores fell.
items.body:
Neural codecs decode speech from compressed latent values, so they can erase a watermark applied to the finished waveform. This system places the message before decoding and trains a detector to recover it after signal processing and codec transformations.

On 48-kilohertz speech passed through EnCodec at 24 kilohertz, codec-aware training increased bit accuracy from 78.8% to 95.6% and 97.1% in two settings. The PESQ speech-quality score fell from 3.727 to 3.514 and 3.427.

The authors present the work as a study of the trade-off, not a universal watermarking system. It is a seven-page preprint with no independent evaluation, and higher message survival came with lower measured quality.
items.why_selected: It makes content provenance concrete: moving a watermark inside the codec can preserve it, but robustness is not free.

citations.title: Investigating Codec-Internal Latent Audio Watermarking for Neural Codec Robustness

items.title: Sonic Stage adds spatial action cues when dialogue blocks audio description
items.summary: Sonic Stage turns dialogue-heavy video into an interactive spatial soundscape for blind and low-vision viewers. A 12-person study found that the added cues improved comprehension, spatial presence, and engagement.
items.body:
Conventional audio description usually waits for gaps in speech, so important actions can disappear from a busy conversation. Sonic Stage instead spatializes each voice, generates sounds tied to visible actions, and lets a viewer request a description for extra context.

The system first reconstructs a stable scene across camera cuts, then maps people and actions into headphone audio. This allows movement and layout to remain audible without placing another continuous narrator over the dialogue.

The evaluation covered 12 blind or low-vision viewers and selected clips. Generated sounds or descriptions can still be wrong, and the paper does not report a production deployment across full films or varied genres.
items.why_selected: It treats accessibility as an audiovisual design problem and uses space, interaction, and sound effects to carry information that narration cannot fit.
